Let’s dive into Chapter 3: Building Lasting Habits Through Small, Sustainable Changes.
Now that you’ve got a better sense of what really matters to you, the next step is figuring out how to actually live by those priorities. Here’s where a lot of people get tripped up—they try to change everything at once. Maybe it’s a brand new diet, a workout plan, and a productivity system, all starting on Monday. Sound familiar?
It’s tempting, but honestly, that approach usually ends in frustration. Why? Because real, lasting change comes from focusing on one habit at a time—and making it so small, it almost feels too easy.
Think of it this way: willpower isn’t endless. If you spread yourself too thin, it just runs out. But if you channel your energy into changing one small thing, you start to build momentum—and your confidence grows right along with it.
Here’s a simple, step-by-step way to create habits that actually stick.
First, pick one habit. Maybe it’s something like taking a ten-minute walk each morning, because that lines up with what’s most important to you.
Next, start small. The goal is to make it so manageable, you can do it even on your busiest day. If you want to run a marathon someday, great—but start by just putting on your running shoes.
Then, tie this new habit to something you already do. That’s called a trigger. For example, right after you brush your teeth or while your coffee’s brewing, you could go for your walk.
Track your progress with a simple checklist or jot it down in a journal. Seeing your streak grow is motivating, even if you’re just ticking off small wins.
And don’t forget to celebrate those wins—no matter how tiny. Give yourself a mental high-five or enjoy a little treat. It keeps you motivated.
Once that new habit feels automatic, that’s when you can start to expand. Maybe you add an extra five minutes to your walk, or you introduce a new habit alongside the first one.
Let’s say you want to read more. Instead of setting a huge goal, just read one page before bed each night. Before you know it, flipping open a book becomes as routine as brushing your teeth—and you can always add more pages later if you want.
Think of this process like building a wall, one brick at a time. Every small success is another brick in the foundation for bigger changes down the line. When you focus on consistency, not intensity, you’re setting yourself up for habits that will actually last.
Of course, there are some common traps to watch out for.
First, don’t try to tackle everything at once. It’s so much better to nail one habit, then move on to the next.
Second, keep your goals realistic. It should feel almost laughably easy at the beginning. That makes it way less intimidating—and much more doable.
And finally, don’t forget about your triggers. If you don’t have a clear prompt to remind you, that new habit can easily slip your mind.
By making small, steady changes, you can reshape your daily routines and make sure your actions truly support your most important priorities. Remember, it’s the little steps done consistently that make the biggest difference in the long run.
